function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repository.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone or push to the repo from here, so you’ll have to run the commands yourself on a machine that has `git`, `docker`, and `kubectl` installed.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo is a simple Node.js (Express) app that listens on port **3000**.  
Create a `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> *Why node:18-alpine?*  
> It’s lightweight, includes Node 18 (the latest LTS at the time of writing), and is a common choice for production Node apps.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (you can create a `k8s/` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use Docker Hub
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip** – If you’re pushing the image to Docker Hub instead of GitHub Container Registry, replace the `image:` line with something like `zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a workflow file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (GCR)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }} \
            .

      # Push the image to GHCR
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
```

> **What this does**  
> * On every push to `main`, it checks out the repo, logs into GHCR using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`, builds the image, tags it with `latest` and the commit SHA, and pushes both tags.  
> If you prefer Docker Hub, replace the login step with `docker/login-action@v3` using your Docker Hub credentials and change the image tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
# Stage the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml

# (Optional) Verify the staged files
git status
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# Commit the changes
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# Push to the remote repo
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run and build/push the Docker image.

---

## Quick sanity check

1. **Build locally** (optional but recommended):

   ```bash
   docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
   ```

   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is running.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (if you have `kubectl` configured):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   ```

   Check the pods:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
   ```

   And expose the service (if you want external access):

   ```bash
   kubectl expose deployment nodejs-welcome-deployment --type=LoadBalancer --name=nodejs-welcome-lb
   ```

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have:

- A production‑ready Dockerfile for the Node.js app  
- Kubernetes deployment & service YAMLs  
- A GitHub Actions workflow that builds and pushes the image on every push to `main`  
- All changes committed and pushed to the repo

Feel free to tweak the image tags, registry, or Kubernetes settings to match your environment. Happy coding!
